newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN urges Ukraine to take steps against torture.
newsitem.headline: UN urges Ukraine to take steps against torture.

text.p: A U.N. rights committee, citing Amnesty International reports of alleged torture by Ukrainian officials during investigations, urged Kiev on Thursday to adopt a new criminal code defining torture as a punishable crime.

The United Nations Committee against Torture, made up of 10 independent experts, also recommended that Ukraine's penal system should be reformed to provide prisoners with greater protection against mistreatment, according to a U.N. statement.

"It noted concern, among other things, over numerous reports by non-governmental organisations alleging use of torture and violence by officials during preliminary investigations and resulting in injuries and -- in some cases -- deaths," it said.

The committee expressed disquiet over "a lack of independent institutions to investigate complaints of torture; over beatings routinely carried out in initiating military recruits; over excessive use of the death penalty in recent years and over a lack of statistical data on numbers of complaints of torture and numbers of persons brought to trial on the basis of those complaints".
They welcomed the Ukraine's adoption last year of a constitution that expressly prohibits torture and urged that a current moratorium on the death penalty be made permanent.

The committee meets twice a year in Geneva to examine compliance with the Convention against Torture and other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment. The 1987 pact has been ratified by 102 states, including Ukraine.
It held a debate on the Ukraine's official report on Tuesday, attended by the former Soviet republic's deputy justice minister, Lada Pavlikovska.

She said that while a "100 percent" description of torture was not contained in Ukrainian legislation, most such offences were banned by laws in effect and carried punishments for perpetrators, according to the U.N. statement.

Violations in places of detention were reacted to as quickly as possible, she added. Some 2,000 officials had been subjected to disciplinary actions and 22 subjected to penal discipline for violations uncovered during 5,000 inspections last year.
Efforts were underway to end the death penalty and no executions had been carried out in 1997, Pavlikovska said.
